abstract: Neuronal translocation is essential for establishing functional tissue architecture in the developing central nervous system. While many of the cell-intrinsic mechanisms driving translocation have been identified, how these strategies adapt to dynamic developmental tissue changes remains less understood. Here, we address this question using retinal Bipolar Cells as a model as they are generated across unlaminated and laminated stages. This enables direct comparison of neuronal translocation modes and dynamics across development. We show that the mode of movement of Bipolar Cells changes depending on tissue lamination state. Bipolar Cells born before photoreceptor layer formation undergo directed, microtubule-dependent somal translocation as seen for other early born neurons. In contrast, later-born Bipolar Cells exhibit more passive and less directed displacement that seems to be mostly driven by collective tissue movements. Interference with tissue-wide movements reduces this displacement, while disrupting photoreceptor layer formation leads to directed translocation also at later developmental stages. Independent of strategy, cells achieve accurate laminar positioning. Together, this shows that tissue context can influence cell movement modes, a principle likely relevant across developing neural and other tissues.
